items.title: [Comment] § 5.6 — pricing[].floor is the offer floor, not the downstream auction floor
items.body:
### Which section?

5.6 — Commercial terms

### Field(s) involved

`pricing[].floor`

### Your comment

The definition — "the lowest rate the seller will consider; enables a `requestable` counter to be evaluated without a round trip" — is the right one, and worth protecting. It is the seller's *offer* floor at proposal time, not the auction-time enforcement floor of the execution standard the line item lands in. For `PREFERRED_DEAL`, `PRIVATE_AUCTION` and `OPEN_AUCTION` mechanisms those are different numbers set by different systems: the exchange sets the bid-request floor per impression, and it moves with the impression.

Suggest one sentence in §5.6 stating that `floor` neither constrains nor describes the downstream auction floor, so that implementers do not wire the two together and a buyer does not read an OpenProposal `floor` as "bids at or above this are guaranteed to clear". (Per-geo shape of the same field is raised separately in #14.)

### Concrete scenario

A buyer commits at `floor` on a private-auction line item. Downstream, the exchange floor on the targeted impressions is higher, so most bids lose. The buyer reads the shortfall as a seller breach of the agreed floor; the seller reads the floor as an offer term that was honoured.

### You are commenting as

SSP — an in-app supply-side exchange (mobile + CTV) selling preferred-deal / private-auction / open-market inventory to buyer agents over AAMP and AdCP; we run the seller side of both today.

### Before you submit

- [x] I have read the draft section I am commenting on.
- [x] This comment contains no confidential or commercially sensitive information.

items.title: Keep one spm_unit_benefits list so reforms that add a benefit stop dropping baseline programs
items.body:
## Problem

`spm_unit_benefits` keeps its list of programs directly in Python, in `policyengine_us/variables/household/income/spm_unit/spm_unit_benefits.py`, not in a parameter. A reform that adds a benefit to SPM resources can't append to that list, so four reforms replace the whole variable with their own copy of it:

- **`reforms/states/tx/rebate/tx_rebate.py`** (#9037) is described as a "verbatim copy of current baseline + `tx_rebate`". Main has since gained `ca_state_supplement`, and the copy doesn't have it.
- **`reforms/congress/tlaib/end_child_poverty_act.py`, `reforms/congress/tlaib/boost/boost_middle_class_tax_credit.py` and `reforms/congress/tlaib/economic_dignity_for_all_agenda/edaa_end_child_poverty_act.py`** are older copies.
  - They lack 28 to 29 of main's entries: every state supplement except Colorado's and Massachusetts's, the Washington and West Virginia programs, and `ak_energy_relief` (missing from two of the three).
  - They still list `acp` and `ebb`, and they use `aca_ptc` where main uses `assigned_aca_ptc`.

When one of these reforms is in effect, its copy replaces `spm_unit_benefits` for every household in the simulation. Any program missing from the copy then drops out of SPM resources in every state, not only in the reform's target group. The reform's SPM net income and poverty results include losses unrelated to the reform.

**Example** (from the review of #10174): once `wy_ssp` is in main, a Wyoming aged SSI-only single in 2027 has `spm_unit_benefits` of 13,202.26 at baseline and 12,962.26 under the Texas rebate reform. The $240 Wyoming supplement disappears.

`tests/test_aggregate_list_integrity.py` checks the reform copies only for contributed programs (added with the Trump dividend fix in ff71e6672b), so missing state programs aren't caught.

## Proposed fix

- Keep the list in one place that both the baseline variable and the reforms read. That could be a module-level list or helper next to `spm_unit_benefits`, or a parameter like `gov.household.household_benefits`.
- Each reform appends only its own program (`tx_rebate`, `ecpa_child_benefit`, `boost_middle_class_tax_credit`) instead of keeping a copy.
- Before replacing the Tlaib copies, check whether their other differences (`acp`, `ebb`, `aca_ptc`) are intended, and keep any intended difference explicit.
- Update `tests/test_aggregate_list_integrity.py` to match, or drop its copy check once no copies remain.

items.title: Magic Mouse handoff leaves a redundant macOS connection-request dialog even though the mouse works
items.body:
## Summary

When I hand off a Magic Mouse between Macs, macOS shows a “Connection Request” dialog even though the mouse has previously been successfully paired.

**The mouse is usable while the dialog is visible.** The handoff has therefore succeeded sufficiently for mouse input; the problem is the redundant confirmation remaining on screen. This is distinct from a peripheral failing to connect or being stranded unpaired.

## Observed behavior

The supplied screenshot shows:

> Connection Request from: Todd’s Magic Mouse
>
> To connect to the device, click Connect to complete the connection process.
>
> To reject connection to the device, click Cancel.

The dialog offers **Ignore this device**, **Cancel**, and **Connect**. Its instruction to finish connecting is confusing because the mouse already works.

![macOS connection request for Todd’s Magic Mouse during a successful handoff](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/176fc0e4-cc41-4dc5-b283-8205c825e87e)

## Reproduction

1. Use a Magic Mouse that has previously been successfully paired.
2. Hand it off between Macs using Magic Switch.
3. Observe the macOS connection-request dialog.
4. Confirm the mouse remains usable without first clicking Connect.

Still to record: macOS versions on both Macs, installed Magic Switch version/build, exact Magic Mouse generation, which Mac displays the dialog, whether both directions are affected, and whether Cancel or Connect changes anything. Do not assume dismissal causes a disconnect; that has not been reported here.

## Expected behavior

An ordinary handoff should complete without leaving a redundant connection request for an already-working, previously paired mouse, wherever supported macOS behavior allows it. The [setup guidance](https://github.com/squizzeak/magic-switch/blob/a3f8bad5511551135e928506552f48567a89485e/README.md#L40-L42) also says users should not need to re-pair manually on every switch.

If macOS requires this dialog in an unavoidable case, document the exact limitation and whether the user needs to act. Do not imply that an already-working mouse still needs to finish connecting.

## Research findings

Reviewed this fork at commit [`a3f8bad`](https://github.com/squizzeak/magic-switch/commit/a3f8bad5511551135e928506552f48567a89485e). This is source review and upstream research, not a local hardware reproduction.

items.title: Echo Show 5 (cronos): a phone can't play to the Show over Bluetooth — no A2DP sink, and with it enabled the kernel drops the link ("Missing AES-CCM usage")
items.body:
### Summary

I wanted any phone to use the Show as a Bluetooth speaker. Two things stand in the way on v1.2.0:

1. **No A2DP sink is registered on the Show.** `t5_bt_up` in `tools/linux/techo5-lib.sh` starts `bluealsa -p a2dp-source` only, so a phone can see the Show but has nothing to play to. (I know "Bluetooth audio as a sink" is on the agreed list in `docs/standalone-plan.md`; reporting what I found trying it, in case it helps.)
2. **With the sink enabled, every connection from the phone is dropped by the kernel** a second or two after it comes up: `Bluetooth: hci0: Invalid security: Missing AES-CCM usage`. Pairing itself works (the passkey is confirmed by techo5's agent), but the stored link key is type 8 (authenticated, P-256) and the encryption change never reports AES-CCM, so `hci_event.c` disconnects.

### Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| Device | Echo Show 5 2nd gen (cronos, C76N8S), MT8163 |
| TECHO5 | rootfs v1.2.0 (2026-10-06T15:46Z), echod v1.2.0 (370716a); v1.2.1/v1.2.2 release notes don't touch Bluetooth |
| Kernel | 4.9.337-g8d928c5176cc |
| BlueZ / bluez-alsa | 5.86 / v4.3.1 |
| Controller (`btmgmt info`) | manufacturer 70 (MediaTek), HCI/LMP version 8 (4.2), through `btbridge`; supported settings include `secure-conn` |
| Phone | Samsung Galaxy S25 Ultra (SM-S938B), Android 16 |

### Steps to reproduce

All changes below were made at runtime over SSH and are lost on reboot.

1. Restart bluez-alsa with both profiles:
   `kill $(pidof bluealsa); bluealsa -p a2dp-source -p a2dp-sink &`
   → `bluetoothctl show` now lists `Audio Sink (0000110b-…)` next to `Audio Source`.
2. Turn on pairing mode (`switch.echoshow_bluetooth_pairing`).
3. On the phone: Bluetooth → pair "EchoShow" → confirm the passkey.
4. Tap "EchoShow" on the phone to connect / play audio to it.

**Expected:** the phone connects and plays through the Show (the receive path in `feature/media/bluetooth.go` + `btaudio` "incoming" looks ready for it).
**Actual:** the phone says "connection error". The link comes up and is dropped every time.

### Logs

techo5 (pairing is fine):
```
I [100076.39] bluetooth pairing confirmed device=/org/bluez/hci0/dev_AA_BB_CC_DD_EE_FF passkey=309583
I [100080.33] bluetooth pairing: a device paired with this one and connected; pairing mode ends address=AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF
```

kernel, once per attempt:
```
[100077.939250] Bluetooth: hci0: Invalid security: Missing AES-CCM usage
[100084.669217] Bluetooth: hci0: Invalid security: Missing AES-CCM usage
```

items.title: [Change] § 5.6 — pricing[].guidance: seller-published transacting-price percentiles alongside floor
items.body:
### What kind of change?

Add a field

### Which section?

5.6 — Commercial terms

### Field(s) involved

`pricing[]` (new OPTIONAL key `guidance`)

### Current text

`pricing[]` entries carry `gross_rate` and an OPTIONAL seller-set `floor` ("the seller's offer floor: the lowest rate it will consider at proposal time", per #16 / PR #18). Nothing describes where the line item actually transacts.

### Proposed text

Add an OPTIONAL, seller-set `pricing[].guidance` object alongside `floor`:

```
pricing: [{
  gross_rate, floor?,
  guidance?: { p25, p50, p75, p90 }   # same units and currency as gross_rate
}]
```

Semantics: the seller's own observed transacting prices for this line item over a seller-chosen trailing window, expressed as percentiles. Like `addressable_scale` (§ 3.3), `guidance` is recomputed against the buyer's current selection when the seller can (e.g. per selected `geo` once #14 part 1 lands), and otherwise describes the line item as offered. It is informational: it creates no obligation and is not an offer.

Suggested field description: "OPTIONAL. Seller-published percentiles of the rates at which this line item has recently transacted, in the units of `gross_rate`. Informational only; a counter at or above `floor` is evaluated on its own terms regardless of `guidance`."

### Why

`floor` tells a buyer the lowest rate the seller will consider; it does not tell the buyer whether a rate above the floor will clear once the line item is live. For exchange-sold inventory those two numbers can be an order of magnitude apart, and they move with the buyer's selection (see the Indonesia / Malaysia example in #14). Without guidance the buyer either overpays to be safe or commits at a rate that cannot clear — the same failure `floor` exists to prevent, one step later.

We publish exactly this on our own catalog today (per-geo p25/p50/p75/p90 next to the floor). It was added after a buyer agent committed a worldwide rate into a market where nothing clears at it; the buyer side asked for it, and it removed that failure mode.

items.title: RFC: compliance run warns on response fields the schema doesn't define, with a suggested name
items.body:
## Problem

A seller agent can misname a field and lose a declaration without anything telling it.

We saw this in production. A seller agent returned this in `get_adcp_capabilities`:

```json
"media_buy": { "supported_buying_modes": ["wholesale", "refine"] }
```

The AdCP field is `media_buy.buying_modes`. Every check let the response through:

- The response validates against the 3.1 schema, because `media_buy` doesn't set `additionalProperties`, so JSON Schema allows any extra key.
- The SDK's strict response validation (`validateResponse` in `@adcp/sdk` 14.1.0) reports it as valid.
- A compliance run against the agent recorded nothing about it.

To a buyer, the agent then has no `buying_modes` declaration. The spec reads an absent declaration as `["brief"]`, so the agent appears not to offer a wholesale catalogue, which is the opposite of what it meant to say. The seller only finds out when a buyer's wholesale path skips them.

Validation catches the same mistake when it is in a value:

| Response `media_buy` | Strict validation (3.1) |
|---|---|
| `{ "buying_modes": ["wholesale", "refine"] }` | valid |
| `{ "supported_buying_modes": ["wholesale", "refine"] }` | **valid**, and the declaration is lost |
| `{ "buying_modes": ["wholesail"] }` | invalid: `must be one of: "brief", "wholesale", "refine"` |

`get_adcp_capabilities` is where this does the most damage, because several of its fields give an absent value a default meaning (`buying_modes`, `require_operator_auth`, the targeting booleans). A misnamed field there doesn't just go missing; it silently turns into the default.

## Proposal

The compliance run should report fields that the schema for the served release doesn't define as **warnings**, with a suggested field name.

1. **Scope.** Check every property the schema doesn't define, at any depth, outside `ext` and `context`. Start with `get_adcp_capabilities`; other responses can follow.
2. **Severity.** Warning only. Never a failed storyboard or a failed baseline. AdCP should keep allowing extra properties so older readers don't break on newer fields.
3. **Suggestion.** When an unknown key is close to a field defined at the same level (by edit distance or shared tokens), name it: `media_buy.supported_buying_modes is not defined in 3.1; did you mean media_buy.buying_modes?`
4. **Version awareness.** A field defined in a later release than the one served is not unknown. Report it as `defined in 3.2, not in served release 3.1` instead. That ties in

items.title: FLEDGE: Parity among players, Accountability, Transparency, and Fraud Detection
items.body:
The present Fledge proposal treats DSPs and SSPs as first class citizens while penalizing other players.

The present proposal also imposes a heavy limit on the ability of any party to hold dsp/ssps accountable and check for fraud. 
Current publishers (or third parties hired by the publishers) using Prebid for example can sum the total bids on a per-event level and compare the total in a given timeframe to the amount the dsp or ssp claims is owed. The Fledge proposal only allows DSPs and SSPs to have this information. 

The question of event or aggregate information is irrelevant (for the moment), the issue is that the DSPs and SSPs monopolize a stream of data that in the interest of transparency should be available to other trusted parties and players.

Trust is insufficient, and publishers often have little recourse to evaluate dsp/ssp systems and even in the current environment when this bid data is only sometimes available there are inconsistencies and issues. Fledge would worsen this problem. Publisher’s can’t merely use dsps/ssps  ‘they trust’ because they cannot establish trust having no way to ensure they are not being cheated. Trust is gained by repeated comparison of auction information in which both sides have similar numbers and can explain any discrepancies. In any other monetary exchange the party owed money is able to determine how much without relying on the party paying.

The publisher, or a publisher trusted agent, should have access to the SAME information the dsps and ssps have. There is no reason to assume that the dsp/ssp would be more trustworthy than a publisher or publisher aid company. Any restriction placed on the data should affect all parties equally and not favor dsps/ssps in particular.

The event based bid data is labeled temporary in the current model, but while it exists, it does not make sense to restrict it to some parties and not others.  

Additionally any aggregate api the dsp/ssp system can access the publisher/publisher trusted agent should also be able to access.

items.title: [FR] Reverse road and resumable sessions: syq receive, ssh-obi, quic-ssh, rose
items.body:
podssh M4 (reverse road) and M6 (sessions that survive) are the largest remaining pieces (`docs/ROADMAP.md`, `docs/reverse.md`). Several sibling projects already ship pieces of this; this FR asks which measured designs to adopt.

Asks:

- **Receiving mode:** an ordinary server reaches a machine with **no SSH server, public address or open port**, over a persistent connection the far side opens. Ref: greaber/syq `docs/receive.md`, `docs/persistence.md`, `src/conn/reverse_tcp.rs` (`begin_reverse_tcp_setup`, one-use `grant`).
- **Resume by byte offset with a bounded replay ring, accepting duplicate recent bytes.** A server keeps the last N bytes with a start offset; the client reconnects and asks from its `received` offset. Ref: VLOD-ZDOV/quic-ssh `src/server/persist.rs:1-38,117,145,268`, `src/client/session.rs:171-310`.
- **Byte-stream replay rather than screen state,** preserving the local terminal's scrollback, with capability negotiation instead of version gating. Ref: menhera-org/ssh-obi README (`replay.v1`, `keepalive.v1`, `initial-window-size.v1`), `src/protocol.rs:17-18`.
- **Reconnect policy:** capped exponential backoff, suspend-aware monotonic deadlines, ping 15 s / pong within 45 s, and the graceful-vs-ambiguous disconnect asymmetry. Ref: ssh-obi README "Ambiguous disconnects reconnect first".
- **SSH bootstrap:** SSH in, start a temporary server, exchange certificates, switch to the fast transport. Ref: nikhiljha/rose `doc/spec.md:172`, `lib/src/cli/ssh_bootstrap.rs`.
- **Lasting terminal via a probed tmux attach.** Ref: ado11231/slingshot `crates/slingshot-agent/src/jobs.rs`, `docs/USAGE.md`.
- **Clean server lifecycle** (kill-server, signals, socket removal, exit notices) for `serve`/`node`. Ref: gold-silver-copper/fux README.

Cross-references: `docs/design.md` §5 (three layers), `docs/ROADMAP.md` M4/M6, `docs/reverse.md`.

I believe that bids should be funneled through an SSP acting on the publisher's behalf, which is less disruptive while accomplishing the privacy goals of TurtleDove/TERN.

## dm_eval finding 3
Same answers going out for different questions:
- "Show me" after a plans answer got the plans text again, 16 seconds later.
- "the drawing" and "picture" did too.
- "Cancel checklist" and "Done" got the same sentence twice.

## Change
`_dm_send_answer` now checks every model answer (`lib/wa_assistant.repeat_of_last`) against Levelog's text answers in this chat from the last **30 minutes**. If the answer matches one of them word for word **and** was given for a **different** question, it is not sent. One short question goes instead:

| Situation | Sent instead |
|---|---|
| The held-back answer cites a sheet | That's what I just sent. Want the drawing — SSP-011.00? Say "show me". |
| Otherwise | That's what I just sent. What should I look at differently? |
| That question was just asked | I'm not getting it — say it another way, or "show me" for the drawing. |

These are logged as path `no_repeat`, with the held-back answer in `repeated`, so the next dm_eval can see them.

**Not a repeat**, so the answer goes out as usual:
- The same question asked again, or reworded with half its content words shared ("open items at 8 walworth" → "and the open items?").
- A **reply-to**: pointing at a message is context, and the same answer about it can be right ("The list", replying to the punch list).

items.title: Spec gap: no specialism for publisher-direct, human-gated, fixed-price, non-guaranteed inventory
items.body:
## Summary

The current specialism taxonomy treats guaranteed/non-guaranteed as a proxy for human-approval/auction. A legitimate seller model falls between the two definitions and has no matching specialism: publisher-direct, fixed-CPM, human-gated (every buy requires publisher approval), non-guaranteed inventory (no reserved impressions, no IO signing).

## The gap

**`sales-non-guaranteed`:** "buyer sets a bid price and budget, the platform runs the auction." Requires auction mechanics, frequency capping, event dedup, clicks/completed-views/audience buying, ROAS optimization. Summary explicitly states "buys don't require IOs or human approval."

**`sales-guaranteed`:** "requires human-in-the-loop IO signing before buys go live." Assumes reserved inventory, proposal flows, guaranteed delivery commitments.

**The model that fits neither:** Fixed-CPM (no auction), publisher-direct (no intermediary), human-gated approval (every buy waits for publisher), non-guaranteed delivery (no reserved impressions, no IO commitment). This is a standard publisher-direct programmatic-guaranteed-adjacent model, but without the reserved-inventory component.

## Why this matters

The combination is not exotic. Publisher-direct ad sales with human approval gates, fixed pricing, and non-guaranteed delivery is the dominant model for mid-market and independent publishers selling direct. The taxonomy's binary (auction = no human approval, guaranteed = human approval) doesn't accommodate it.

## Concrete reproduction

Agent: `https://sell.nofluffadvisory.com`
- `create_media_buy` succeeds, buy enters `pending_approval` state
- Publisher reviews and approves before any delivery
- Fixed CPM, no bid price, no auction
- Non-guaranteed delivery — no reserved impressions, no IO signing
- `sales-non-guaranteed` declared (incorrectly, now being corrected)
- `sales-guaranteed` doesn't fit — no reserved inventory or proposal flow

The `capability_unsupported` skips on `audience_buy_flow`, `clicks_buy_flow`, `completed_views_buy_flow`, `event_dedup_flow`, `frequency_cap_enforcement` are honest declarations — we don't implement these because the model doesn't require them. But they're all in `sales-non-guaranteed`'s `requires_scenarios`, making the specialism uncertifiable without building capabilities the product doesn't need.

## Suggested resolution

Add a specialism that describes the publisher-direct, human-gated, fixed-price, non-guaranteed model — or decouple the human-approval axis fro

items.title: LuneOS.Bluetooth: don't let a stuck rfkill switch disable Bluetooth
items.body:
## Tapping a Bluetooth device does nothing when an rfkill switch is stuck

BluezQt's `Manager::isBluetoothOperational()` requires **every** Bluetooth rfkill switch to be unblocked: its global state is the worst one across all of them. On the BlackBerry KEY2 (athena, WCN3990), the vendor `bt_power` switch never unblocks. The chip has no enable GPIO, so the kernel logs `bluetooth_power: bt_power gpio config failed` on every attempt. The Android HAL powers the chip through `/dev/btpower` instead, and Bluetooth itself works (`hci0` is unblocked and the adapter powers on).

`BluetoothManager.bluetoothOperational` was therefore always false, which caused three problems:
- **Taps did nothing:** `connectDeviceAddress()` returned without doing anything. Tapping a device in Settings → Bluetooth (or the system menu) made no D-Bus call to BlueZ at all.
- **No pairing agent:** the Settings page registers its agent on `bluetoothOperationalChanged`, which never fired.
- **"Init" forever:** the system menu showed **Init** instead of **On**, because `initializing` is `powered && !bluetoothOperational`.

### Change

`bluetoothOperational` now means BluezQt is operational and has a usable adapter. `connectDeviceAddress()` checks this property rather than BluezQt's own flag.

Whether Bluetooth is on is still decided by connman (`powered`). When connman powers the adapter off, BluezQt no longer offers it as the usable adapter, so the rfkill check added nothing on devices where it works.

### Testing

On a BlackBerry KEY2 (athena), image `athena_20260930`, with this file in place of the shipped one:

- **Before:**
  - `dbus-monitor` showed no call from the Settings app to `org.bluez` when tapping a device;
  - BluezQt reported `bluetoothBlocked=true`;
  - the system menu said "Init".
- **After:**
  - opening Settings → Bluetooth calls `AgentManager1.RegisterAgent`;
  - tapping an unpaired headset calls `Device1.Pair()` (SSP pairing completed) and then `Device1.Connect()`;
  - after a reboot the system menu says **On**, and the paired headset reconnected on its own.

Getting audio to the headset also needed PulseAudio's Bluetooth module, which is not loaded on the default config (webOS-ports/meta-webos-ports#836). A dual-mode headset can still end up connected over LE only (webOS-ports/meta-webos-ports#835); this PR doesn't address that.

## What and why

New Jersey's optional SSI supplement was missing from PolicyEngine-US. Add `nj_ssp` with the verified 2026 rates for each New Jersey living arrangement code, including the special rate for a recipient who lives only with an ineligible spouse.

The calculation uses the shared SSI state supplement helper (`_ssi_state_supplement.py`, identical to the copy in the sibling state SSP PRs). It handles the income reduction, couple halving, spouse-to-spouse deeming, SSA cent rounding and the $1 minimum. Under deeming it uses the higher individual rate, because New Jersey's individual rates exceed its couple rates in codes B and C. The supplement follows SSI eligibility and take-up, because SSA pays it with the federal benefit. Add it to household and SPM benefit totals and to SNAP and HUD unearned income.

Some situations need explicit inputs:
- a couple who buys food separately from others at the same address, or lives only with foster children;
- certified congregate care and residential health care settings;
- spouses who claim as individuals after the month they enter a facility.

Every rate except the Medicaid-facility rate includes New Jersey's Lifeline utility payment. #10230 tracks counting the supplement net of the Lifeline in New Jersey LIHEAP.

The files live under `gov/states/nj/njdhs/ssp`, next to New Jersey's other Department of Human Services programs.

items.body:
#### Description, the reason for the PR

When an online payment fails on the gateway, the customer is offered to repeat it in the order detail and in the order list. Until now that offer stayed even after an administrator cancelled the order, and the customer could still open the payment gateway and pay for an order that no longer exists. Cancelling an order now ends its payment flow. items.title: User programs use AVX to AVX-512, saved by the best XSAVE form each CPU offers
items.body:
Takes up `issues/user-programs-use-avx-under-xsave.md`. The owner's rulings: "ToyOS is modern, so AVX is needed", and ToyOS supports every modern x86 CPU, using the best save form each CPU offers. Until now `CR4.OSXSAVE` stayed clear and a thread's state was its `FXSAVE64` image, so every AVX instruction in a user program was `#UD`. With this branch a user program gets AVX, and AVX-512 where the CPU has it, and std's `is_x86_feature_detected!` reports both from CPUID and `XCR0` as it does on Linux. Each CPU saves that state with XSAVES, XSAVEC or XSAVEOPT, chosen at boot from its CPUID. No ABI change.

Head: `cbf8e09e4`, five commits and two merges of `origin/main` on `57616a067`:
- `f7b497231` turns on XSAVE, with XSAVEOPT on every CPU;
- `386631a16` fixes the XSAVEOPT invariant the T14 and the AMD bench broke at `f7b497231` (*Hardware*);
- `1bcfdb781` makes the save form per CPU, by the owner's ruling (*Save form*);
- `063f72b73` answers the third review: erratum 1386 becomes `toyos-cpuvuln`'s verdict, scoped by AMD's revision guides; an unknown form is `ud2`; three issues filed;
- `cbf8e09e4` touches one issue only: it records in the `consent_prompt` defect that both of its red 20 s waits are a fixed `Duration::from_secs(20)` (`Consent::begin`, `Consent::prompt_up`) that the harness never passes through `qemu::budget_smp`. No code changes, so every kernel and metal reading at `063f72b73` holds for `cbf8e09e4`.

The design was accepted on the pull request after it was built: https://github.com/ToyOSOrg/ToyOS/pull/859#issuecomment-6113969744.

## Design

### State components (`XCR0`)

| bit | component | decision |
|---|---|---|
| 0, 1 | x87, SSE | required |
| 2 | AVX (YMM_Hi128) | **required**, per the ruling: a CPU without it is refused by name |
| 5, 6, 7 | opmask, ZMM_Hi256, Hi16_ZMM | **on, as one group, where the CPU enumerates all three** (SDM Vol. 1 §13.3: `XCR0` takes them together); a CPU that enumerates part of the group is refused by name |
| 3, 4 | MPX | off: deprecated |
| 9 | PKRU | off: needs `CR4.PKE`, which `issues/user-programs-have-no-protection-keys.md` owns |
| 17, 18 | AMX | off: 8 KiB per save. The T14 has none: its `CPUID.(0DH,0).EAX` is `0x2e7` (`kernel/cpuvuln/fixtures/t14/cpuid.txt`) |
| 19+ | APX and later | off until a decision names them |

The decision is `kernel::xsave::xcr0` (`kernel/pure/xsave.rs`), a pure function over CPUID words. The T14 gets `0xe7`, TCG and an AVX-only AMD part `0x7`. It also refuses a CPU without X

items.body:
## What changed, and why

After Elyse approved the first live chat booking (2026-10-11), the readable card turned into `Applied · Create 1 deal on Index Exchange …` above forty lines of raw JSON. The deal's two ids and its link were only inside that JSON. This PR builds the designer's completed card ("Approval Flow and Card Requirements", pages 9–11) and the pending card's mockup layout. All of it is opt-in.

**1. A bundle can have chosen tools report their own outcome card.**

```yaml
agent_policy:
  critical_tools: [execute_plan, next_campaign_id]
  critical_tool_result_cards: [execute_plan, next_campaign_id]
```

- **The result carries the card.** A member tool's result JSON may include a top-level `result_card`. It holds an `outcome` (`done|partial|failed|mismatch|unclear`), a `title`, and `items`, each with `label`, `status` (`done|failed|mismatch|unclear|skipped|not_run`), `key`, `id`, `internal_id`, `link`, `link_label` and `note`, plus changes, settings and flags. It can also carry `retry.keys`. The full schema is in `docs/APPROVAL-RESULT-CARDS.md`.
- **Fleet reads it once, after governance.** When the approved call returns and passes governance, fleet reads the card from the governed text before the size bound, so a long batch result is still read whole. Fleet makes **no second call**.
- **Strict checks.** The checks are ADR-0082's: strict decode, no nulls, text-only rules, https-only links, and the same limits. Two extra rules apply:
  - The outcome may not contradict the rows. A `done` card has no failed, mismatched or unclear rows. A `failed` card has no applied rows.
  - A retry may name only `failed` or `not_run` rows of the card, so never an unclear or mismatched create.
  - A value the secret redaction would alter refuses the card.

items.title: Detect a controller with Bluetooth LE switched off and explain how to turn it on
items.body:
Related to #192

## Summary

Setup now detects a controller that supports Bluetooth LE but runs with it switched off. Full-mode pairing re-probes twice and then stops with an actionable message before any pairing transaction. Before, it bonded over Classic and then failed with "The ANCS advertisement did not activate". `blueferry doctor` runs the same check.

BlueFerry does **not** switch LE on itself. An earlier revision shipped a unit that ran `btmgmt le on`; that was removed after review, because under `ControllerMode = bredr` bluetoothd has no LE advertising manager for the adapter until it restarts (see Design). The message tells the user what does work, and the CLI wizard and the KDE client offer to check again after the user restarted bluetoothd.

## Why

The #192 report (Broadcom BCM2045A0, `0a5c:6412`, HCI 7, BlueZ 5.87) shows:

- `supported_settings` contains `le` and `advertising`.
- `current_settings` contains only `br/edr powered secure-conn ssp`.
- `phone.le_bearer.present` is false.
- `advert_unavailable` comes 2 ms after `advert_register_sent`.

The controller can do LE, but BlueZ is running it Classic-only. The most likely cause is `ControllerMode = bredr` in `/etc/bluetooth/main.conf`. `_profile_fields` only looked at the supported settings, so the adapter counted as fully capable and the failure appeared late, with a message that doesn't point at the cause.

This is a different cause from #188–#191 (legacy BlueZ without bearer interfaces, legacy-sized advertisement retry). Here the controller's LE setting is off, so no advertisement of any size can register. This PR touches the same functions as #191 in a few places (`_profile_fields`, `derive_stage`, `BluetoothCompatibility`, `pair_setup`, `setup_client`), with small, separate additions; whichever lands second needs a short rebase.

## Design

- **Detection** (`bluetooth_capabilities.py`):
  - `_profile_fields` adds `le_enabled` (`le` in current) and `le_disabled` (probe available, LE supported, not current).
  - `compatibility()` adds `controller_mode`, read from `[General] ControllerMode` in `/etc/bluetooth/main.conf` with the same rules as bluetoothd's GKeyFile + `strcmp` (case-sensitive names, whole-line `#` comments only, value verbatim, a rejected line means bluetoothd ignores the file). Only `dual`/`bredr`/`le`/`other` is reported, never raw text.

items.body:
## Paper and artifact status

**Christopher H. Lin, Andrey Kolobov, Ece Kamar, and Eric Horvitz, “Metareasoning for Planning Under Uncertainty.”** Proceedings of IJCAI 2015, July 2015, pp. 1601–1607. The arXiv version was submitted 3 May 2015.

- [Official Microsoft Research record](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/metareasoning-planning-uncertainty/)
- [Official IJCAI paper](https://www.ijcai.org/Proceedings/15/Papers/229.pdf)
- [Extended paper with appendix](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/wp-content/uploads/2016/11/1505.00399v1.pdf)
- [arXiv:1505.00399](https://arxiv.org/abs/1505.00399)

I did not find an author-provided code artifact. That limits reproducibility of the approximate BRTDP controller and of the synthetic-domain results.

This fills a different gap from recent issues:

- #115 learns a gate between acting and a finite menu of planning depths, while planning is represented primarily by its scalar compute cost.
- #116 handles an external planner whose delayed answer may become stale while the agent continues to act.
- #117 studies concurrent computation across incompatible plan branches and the option value destroyed by dispatch.
- #129 separates uncertainty about the environment from uncertainty caused by incomplete planning.

Lin et al. provide the useful foundational bridge among these ideas: **make the planner’s internal configuration part of the decision state, and make another unit of thinking an ordinary action whose transition can change both the planner and the world.** Their approximation then asks whether the observed progress of an anytime solver justifies one more cycle.

## Established technical idea

### An exact meta-MDP in which thinking can move the world

The base problem is a stochastic shortest-path MDP

`M = <S, A, T, C, s0, sg>`

1. **act:** execute `f(s, χ)`; the world changes and the solver configuration is frozen;

items.body:
## What changed, and why

Interactive chat gains a **`show_ui`** tool. It is fleet's version of the "generative UI" pattern ChatGPT shipped as *Intelligent UI* on Oct 7. When a visual or interactive answer serves the user better than prose, the agent builds a card on the spot from a fixed component catalog, and the web chat renders it inline. A card can be:

- a form, or a multi-step form with tabs
- a picker over options the agent fetched from MCP tools
- a multi-item editor (add / duplicate / remove)
- allow/block lanes, or a paste-a-list input
- a pass/fail checklist with **Fix** links
- a proposed-changes diff, a selectable table, a bar or line chart, or a live calculator

The motivating case is the big AI-assisted intake form, such as a multi-SSP deal builder. With this, the agent composes that form per turn from the MCP servers it can reach, validates the answers against the live systems, and re-shows the card with field errors (`replaces` + `field_errors`). It then creates the deals with its normal tools. Nothing in fleet knows about deals; a bundle can teach the pattern with a skill.

**How it works**
- **The card is declarative data, never code** ([ADR-0080](docs/adr/0080-generative-ui-cards-are-declarative-data.md)).
  - `internal/genui` validates every spec at tool-call time: catalog, props, ids, value types, option sets, card-wide render budgets, the smallest answer a validating submit must send, and expression syntax and references. A mistake comes back as a tool error naming each path, so the model fixes it in the same turn.
  - A card whose text (raw or JSON-decoded) would be altered by secret redaction is refused, so the user never sees a card that differs from what was validated.
  - The renderer draws only catalog components and treats every string as text. Its one markdown surface allows no raw HTML or images, it opens only `https` links (with `noopener`), and it fetches nothing on render.
  - The only logic is a small, side-effect-free expression language: `{{ }}` templates, `visible_if`, `disabled_if`. ## What changed

The reviewer's two remaining website recommendations — *experimental status beside the CTA* and *make the working assessment flow the primary demo* — plus a broken test suite found on the way.

### The preview status, beside the button

Nothing on the site said what this build is. The homepage, the assessors page, the 20x walkthrough and the demo itself now carry one line where a visitor decides whether to click:

> **PUBLIC PREVIEW** — **Experimental.** Every determination here is automated EXAMINE preparation for an assessor to check — never an authorization decision. Thank you for your attention to [TURTLEDOVE](https://github.com/michaelkleber/turtledove) and your desire to improve on it!  To help me understand SPARROW, let me ask some questions about the flow of information between the browser, the Gatekeeper, and the ad network.

For the purposes of this Issue, I'll assume that everyone agrees that the Gatekeeper is perfectly trustworthy.

> At that point, the ad network calls regular DSPs for contextual bids and the browser calls the Gatekeeper with interest groups and page contextual data.

Does this mean the "contextual data" is all computed by the browser and the publisher's ad network?  In TURTLEDOVE, by contrast, it's possible for each DSP to learn the URL of the page and compute its own contextual signals ([discussion](https://github.com/michaelkleber/turtledove/issues/20#issuecomment-602800377)).

## What and why (finding A-09, P1; the create/update half. The delete half is #500)

`POST /v1/agents` answered 201 for an agent whose `model.profile_id` and `tools` named things that do not exist. `GET /v1/agents/{id}/status` then said so, and the agent failed at its first turn, with nothing at the point of creation to say why. The builder agent is the principal most likely to get a profile or toolset id wrong, and the system `create_agent` tool and the builder's `crud` toolset had the same gap.

Now one shared check runs before the write on all three surfaces (the REST route, the system `create_agent` / `update_agent` tools, the builder's `crud` toolset):

- `model.profile_id` must name a stored ModelProfile: 422 `model_profile_not_found`, field `model.profile_id`.
- Every toolset the `tools` name must resolve: 422 `toolset_not_found`, field `tools`, every missing id named once and sorted. A tool id's toolset is the part before its LAST `__` (an id with no `__` is its own toolset, the rule `/status` has always applied). It resolves when it is an in-process built-in (`RESERVED_TOOLSET_IDS`, after a retired `_system`-style id is mapped to its current one) or a stored Toolset row. `search` is a stored row, not a built-in.

correct and well-built primitive: immutable bytes bound by `content_sha256`,
`base_sha256` for CAS, `author`, `decided_by`, invisible to every read path by
construction rather than by exclusion rules.

Two things it cannot express:

1. **A run is usually more than one page.** An inbox agent filing a call

   updates a decision record. Today that is three independent drafts, promoted
   one at a time, each with its own CAS. A reviewer who promotes two and

2. **Promotion is all-or-nothing against a stale CAS.** If the target page moved

## What changed, and why

A person can now **leave records out of one approved call**. A deal plan books one `<ssp>_execute_plan(deal_ids=[…])` per system, and one call covers many deals. Grouped approvals let a trader drop a whole call, but not one deal inside it, so they ticked deals on a separate review card and then approved a second card. The designer's states 2, 2b, 2c, 2d ("uncheck any deal to leave it out", "Left out" rows) put review and approval on one card.

```yaml
agent_policy:
  critical_tool_card_describers: {execute_plan: describe_plan_call}
  critical_tool_narrowable_args:
    execute_plan: {arg: deal_ids}
```

# RFC: First-Class TMP Support in Prebid Server

Status: Draft for discussion
Target repos: `prebid/prebid-server`, `prebid/prebid-server-java`
Related repos: `prebid/salesagent`, `prebid/prebid.github.io`
Authors: TBD
Last updated: 2026-07-03

## Summary

This RFC proposes making the Trusted Match Protocol (TMP) router a first-class Prebid Server capability in both PBS-Go and PBS-Java.

TMP should be exposed as an open, publisher-friendly Prebid surface for package activation and trusted matching. It should run in the same operational path as existing Prebid Server deployments, use equivalent external configuration in Go and Java, and preserve TMP's core privacy property: context matching and identity matching are separate operations whose results are joined locally by publisher infrastructure.

This proposal is complementary to, not a rejection of, IAB Tech Lab's Agentic Real Time Framework (ARTF). ARTF defines a broad containerized framework for agent services that can operate inside a host platform's real-time bidstream. TMP in Prebid Server should provide a narrower, Prebid-native, open-source path for publishers who want trusted package activation without adopting a general third-party container execution framework.

## Recent Public Context

As of 2026-07-03, the public standards context has moved in a way that strengthens this RFC:

- AdCP's TMP web-publisher guide now explicitly describes TMP as a Prebid module that replaces vendor-specific RTD modules with one standard protocol. At repository baseline `46e2427beca074fa4aa8ff4a12cedec158ab401d`, hmc-mcp registers 156 MCP tools (155 exposed by default), but tool count does not establish command/API completeness or hardware verification. # ArXiv Paper Summaries (2026-09-29)

Found 282 relevant papers.

Papers 181-190 of 282 (Part 19/29).

## GuidedRay: Diversity-Guided Direction Discovery for Targeted Hard-Label Black-Box Attacks
**Authors:** Fei Yuan, Yantian Shen, Qingyuan Yu, Yi Chen, Binghui Wang, Hongbo Yu, Anyu Wang, Xiaoyun Wang

### Summary
**Problem:** Targeted decision-based (hard‑label) black-box attacks must force a model to predict a prespecified target class with only top‑1 label feedback. The main bottleneck is initialization: efficiently discovering a sign-direction that reaches the target region in high-dimensional L∞ sign space, where naive or untargeted directions rarely succeed and query budgets are tight.

**Proposed Method:** GuidedRay, a two-phase attack focused on diversity-guided, target-conditioned direction discovery. In initialization, the Adversarial Direction Search Framework (ADSF) generates varied target-conditioned candidates from one or more target-class reference images via augmentations (Gaussian noise, rotation, crop-resize, color jitter). Each candidate is mapped to a discrete sign direction relative to the benign input, and a one-query Fast Test probes a single point on the induced ray to certify feasibility; successful directions undergo a short binary search to set the initial radius. This promotes diverse, target-informed directions while avoiding costly boundary searches for non-viable candidates. In optimization, the attack adopts Ray Search (RayS) to refine the decision-boundary radius within the same discrete sign space. GuidedRay supports single- and multi-reference settings and includes an untargeted variant that seeds candidates from augmented versions of the benign input.

**Key Results:** Across CIFAR-10/ResNet-50, CIFAR-100/ResNet-50, and ImageNet/DenseNet-121, GuidedRay consistently achieves the highest targeted ASR at query budgets 500, 1K, 3K, and 5K, with especially large gains in initialization. items.title: RFC: let outcome_target carry a cost target and a vendor-metric goal
items.body:
## Working-group proposal

Let a buyer's `criteria.outcome_target` carry the cost it is willing to pay and a vendor-measured goal, so the request-time objective can say the same thing the package-level `optimization-goal` and the proposal's `optimization_goals[]` already can.

## Problem

`outcome_target` (media-buy/outcome-target.json, landed in #6728) is deliberately compact: one `goal` (a `forecastable-metric` or an `event-type`) plus a `volume`. The seller solves for budget and answers with `total_budget_guidance` and a forecast whose points carry the goal key (#6745 restored that answer path on the canonical proposal).

Two common buyer asks cannot be stated at request time:

1. **A cost ceiling.** "I want clicks at €3 or less, €5k budget" has no home. The buyer must pre-compute `volume: 1667` and drop the ceiling. The seller then cannot tell "1,667 clicks" apart from "as many clicks as you can at ≤ €3", and cannot answer "I can do €4.50 but not €3". The package-level `optimization-goal` already has `target: { kind: 'cost_per' | 'threshold_rate' | 'per_ad_spend' }`, so the vocabulary exists one step later in the lifecycle but not where planning happens.
2. **A vendor-measured outcome.** "Store visits, measured by Placer" is expressible as a package goal (`kind: 'vendor_metric'`, `vendor: BrandKey`, `metric_id`) and as a delivery value (`vendor_metric_values[]`), and forecast points already carry `vendor_metric_values[]` (`ForecastVendorMetricValue`). But `outcome_target.goal` only has `metric` and `event` branches, and `forecastable-metric` excludes every outcome metric (`foot_traffic`, `units_sold`, `conversions`, `roas`, `incremental_sales_lift` are all in `available-metric` but not in `forecastable-metric`). So the one goal a retailer or QSR most wants to plan against cannot be asked for.

The result is that a buyer agent has to carry the real objective in the free-text `brief` and hope the seller reads it, which is the failure `outcome_target` was added to remove.

## Proposed direction

Both changes are additive and mirror shapes that already exist elsewhere in the spec.

**1. Optional `target` on `outcome_target`**, using the same target kinds as `optimization-goal`:

```jsonc
{
  "goal": { "kind": "metric", "metric": "clicks" },
  "target": { "kind": "cost_per", "value": 3.00 },
  "volume": 1667            // becomes optional when target is present
}
```

Answer semantics: with `volume` only, the seller answers with budget guidance (unchanged).

> **Draft until bench-verified.** This PR previously carried the SMP mode 0x49 (LE Secure Connections) change, which was **bench-tested and proven inert** — every LE bond still paired legacy. ## Root cause (confirmed by direct observation)

nRF Connect on an advertising Shimmer3R shows the auto-generated LE advertisement's Flags AD = `0x06`: *LE General Discoverable* + **"BR/EDR Not Supported"**. The sensor itself tells every scanner it has no classic side. Android obeys: LE-only bond, no classic SDP, no cached `SPP` — and Chrome's Android serial picker (which enumerates from cached SDP records) can never list the sensor.

Take over the advertisement content, **replicating the module's own packets byte-for-byte with exactly one byte changed** — Flags `0x06 → 0x02`:

- adv: `02 01 02` · `11 07 <CYSPP service UUID>` · `07 FF 3101 00000000` (Cypress MSD + zeroed CYSPP key) — 29 bytes

items.title: feat(api): warn when a group's parameters are fixed by default
items.body:
You asked that an undefined parameter not be silent, and that the parameter list be shown. This does that without changing what any model does.

## The silence

```python
SEDModel.build(ssp_data=ssp, observation=obs, redshift=Fixed(0.5),
               sfh={"type": "dpl"})          # no 'all_params'
# -> model.spec.n_free == 0, and not one warning
```

The user believes they configured an SFH and gets a model with none of it free. The `FIXED` default is documented and correct and is **unchanged**; only the silence is.

## What you now see

```
Group 'sfh' states no 'all_params' disposition, so its remaining 5 parameters
were fixed at declared defaults:
  sfh_dpl_age_gyr=13.81, sfh_dpl_alpha=1.5, sfh_dpl_beta=1,
  sfh_dpl_log_total_mass=10, sfh_dpl_tau_gyr=3

To fit them, pass 'all_params': FREE:
  sfh={'all_params': FREE, ...}
To keep them fixed and silence this warning, say so explicitly:
  sfh={'all_params': FIXED, ...}
```

One warning per group, not per parameter. Parameters and their pinned values are listed (first eight, then a count). Explicit `all_params` either way, and explicit per-parameter `Fixed(...)`, stay silent: those are the user saying what they want. `DefaultFixedParametersWarning` subclasses the existing `AdvisoryWarning`, so it can be filtered precisely.

## Two things the first pass got wrong, found by review

**Wrong group named.** For `high_z` and `photoz` the warning said group `'sfh'` and then listed `met_alpha_fe`, `met_logzsol_scatter`. Those are metallicity parameters; they sit in the `sfh` partition only when the user passed no `met` block, by design (#311/#1720). The message therefore named a group the user never wrote and offered a remedy that does not apply, since `sfh={'all_params': FIXED}` says nothing about metallicity. They are now excluded: naming the wrong group is worse than staying quiet.

**Claimed "all".** The message said "all parameters are silently fixed" for groups that set several parameters explicitly. It now states only the count that actually defaulted, and the test asserts the requirement rather than a particular phrasing.

## Shipped recipes were about to warn their own users

`high_z` (2 warnings), `photoz` (2) and `mock_recovery_minimal` (1) relied on the silent default, so every user of the blessed path would have been warned about a choice the recipe author made. They now state `'all_params': FIXED` explicitly, which also makes them self-documenting.

Proven a no-op by resolving every buildable recip

 - **Abstract**
 Speech emotion recognition (SER) processes speech signals to detect and characterize expressed perceived emotions. Many SER application systems often acquire and transmit speech data collected at the client-side to remote cloud platforms for inference and decision making. However, speech data carry rich information not only about emotions conveyed in vocal expressions, but also other sensitive demographic traits such as gender, age and language background. Consequently, it is desirable for SER systems to have the ability to classify emotion constructs while preventing unintended/improper inferences of sensitive and demographic information. Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning paradigm that coordinates clients to train a model collaboratively without sharing their local data. This training approach appears secure and can improve privacy for SER. However, recent works have demonstrated that FL approaches are still vulnerable to various privacy attacks like reconstruction attacks and membership inference attacks. Although most of these have focused on computer vision applications, such information leakages exist in the SER systems trained using the FL technique. To assess the information leakage of SER systems trained using FL, we propose an attribute inference attack framework that infers sensitive attribute information of the clients from shared gradients or model parameters, corresponding to the FedSGD and the FedAvg training algorithms, respectively. As a use case, we empirically evaluate our approach for predicting the client's gender information using three SER benchmark datasets: IEMOCAP, CREMA-D, and MSP-Improv. ## Keyword: SLAM
### WOLF: A modular estimation framework for robotics based on factor graphs
 - **Authors:** Joan Sola, Joan Vallve-Navarro, Joaquim Casals, Jeremie Deray, Mederic Fourmy, Dinesh Atchuthan, Juan Andrade-Cetto
 - **Subjects:** Robotics (cs.RO)
 - **Arxiv link:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.12919
 - **Pdf link:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2110.12919
 - **Abstract**
 This paper introduces WOLF, a C++ estimation framework based on factor graphs and targeted at mobile robotics. WOLF extends the applications of factor graphs from the typical problems of SLAM and odometry to a general estimation framework able to handle self-calibration, model identification, or the observation of dynamic quantities other than localization. WOLF produces high throughput estimates at sensor rates up to the kHz range, which can be used for feedback control of highly dynamic robots such as humanoids, quadrupeds or aerial manipulators. Departing from the factor graph paradigm, the architecture of WOLF allows for a modular yet tightly-coupled estimator. Modularity is based on plugins that are loaded at runtime. Then, integration is achieved simply through YAML files, allowing users to configure a wide range of applications without the need of writing or compiling code. Synchronization of incoming data and their processing into a unique factor graph is achieved through a decentralized strategy of frame creation and joining. Most algorithmic assets are coded as abstract algorithms in base classes with varying levels of specialization. Overall, these assets allow for coherent processing and favor code reusability and scalability. WOLF can be interfaced with different solvers, and we provide a wrapper to Google Ceres. Likewise, we offer ROS integration, providing a generic ROS node and specialized packages with subscribers and publishers. WOLF is made publicly available and open to collaboration.

items.title: spec(creative): add IAB CTV experience profiles for AdCP 3.2
items.body:
## Problem

AdCP 3.2 needs to describe CTV home/menu and high-impact screen experiences. The IAB Tech Lab CTV Ad Portfolio defines six such experiences beyond linear (Menu including home screen, Pause, Screensaver, Overlay, Squeezeback, In-Scene), and its [signaling guidelines](https://github.com/InteractiveAdvertisingBureau/Ad-Format-Guidelines-for-Digital-Video-CTV/blob/main/Signaling-Implementation-Guidelines.md) map Menu to OpenRTB Native and the other five to VAST `<NonLinearAds>`.

An earlier draft of this RFC hard-wired that table as AdCP's creative-ingestion contract (Menu → `native_in_feed` only; the other five → `video_vast` only, with invalid pairings failing validation). Checking published platform specs falsifies that as an ingestion model:

- No fetched platform ingests NonLinear VAST for these placements today. [Disney GatewayGo](https://products.disneyadvertising.com/gatewaygo/): "We cannot serve through VAST tags. Must be site-served." Netflix pause ads are static-image-only. Roku Action Ads take proprietary template parameters via direct upload.
- Menu heroes are video-mandatory with focus-triggered autoplay ([Fire TV Feature Rotator](https://advertising.amazon.com/resources/ad-specs/fire-tv/feature-rotator), [Samsung 1st Screen Masthead](https://help.dsp.samsungads.com/docs/1st-screen-masthead)) — but `native_in_feed` has no video slot and its scope text routes video-first native elsewhere.
- Interaction contracts (Samsung Virtual Tune-In, Roku OK-to-Text, GatewayGo push/email/QR copy, Google TV deep-link hierarchy) are neither VAST events nor Native 1.2 assets.
- Fire TV Sponsored Tiles behave as catalog listings — `sponsored_placement` territory the earlier draft ignored.

The IAB mapping is real and final — but it is an **OpenRTB signaling standard**, not a creative-supply contract. AdCP should preserve it as the bridge annex and model creative supply on what sellers ingest.

### 1. Shared `ctv_ad_experience` vocabulary (unchanged)

```text
menu | pause | screensaver | overlay | squeezeback | in_scene
```

Jeff – Jev-compatible 0.8B decision models, trained at home, ~30 ms # Jeff：轻量级、快速决策模型系列概述 Jeff 是一系列基于 Qwen3.5 和 Gemma 4 微调的小型决策模型（参数规模为 0.8B 和 2B），旨在为开发者提供极速、高准确度且经过校准的**零样本分类（Zero-shot Classification）**能力。这些模型可以直接集成到本地代码中，通过单次前向传播返回选项的概率，无需生成文本或进行复杂的解析。 ### 核心特性 * **极速响应**：决策延迟极低。在 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 上约为 22 ms，在 Apple M4 Max (MLX) 上约为 28 ms。 * **零样本决策**：用户只需用自然语言描述场景和选项，模型即可进行选择。选项内容无需出现在训练数据中，适用于支持队列分类、用户意图识别、内容审核、语音命令等多种场景。 * **高效输出**：模型直接返回每个选项的校准概率、选定的选项及置信度。支持三种提问类型： * `choice`：从最多 254 个选项中选择一个（v1.1 Qwen 模型）。 * `noul`：回答“是/否”问题（返回概率）。 * `score`：按描述的尺度进行评分。 * **高度可定制**：虽然具备强大的零样本能力，但通过少量样本进行微调可以显著提升特定领域的准确率（例如：语音导航任务从 31.7% 提升至 95.8%）。 ### 版本迭代 (v1.1 更新) 2026 年 9 月发布的 v1.1 版本针对以下方面进行了重大改进： * **长列表支持**：支持多达 254 个选项（v1.0 仅支持 26 个）。0.8B 模型在长列表测试中的准确率从 40% 大幅提升至 95%。 * **校准优化**：显著降低了校准误差，使概率输出更加可靠。 ### 性能表现 * **基准测试**：在分类和 grounding 任务上，Jeff 的表现接近甚至在某些指标上超过了大型模型 Jev。但在需要复杂逻辑推理的任务（如 BBH、JudgeBench）中，受限于参数规模，其表现仍低于大型模型。 * **游戏测试**：在零样本测试中，Jeff-0.8B 在 Doom、Frogger 和 Pac-Man 等游戏场景中展现了比未经训练的模型更强的决策能力。 * **微调案例**：通过在 60 万个国际象棋位置上进行微调，Jeff-0.8B 的解题准确率从零样本的 15.5% 提升到了 55.8%。 ### 技术实现与训练 * **本地化训练**：整个训练过程完全在本地硬件（如单块 RTX PRO 6000）上完成，不依赖云端 GPU。 * **合成数据**：使用开源模型（Qwen3.8-Flash-Next）生成合成训练数据，并配合泄漏过滤器（leak filter）确保数据质量。 * **训练流程**：采用全权重微调（Full-weight fine-tuning），进行单轮 epoch 训练，通过交叉熵损失函数结合温度校准（temperature calibration）来优化输出。 ### 使用建议与注意事项 * **适用场景**：Jeff 是一个**分类器**而非**规划器**。它擅长根据当前状态做出快速决策，但不擅长预测复杂后果或进行多步推理。 * **提示词工程**：选项的措辞对结果影响极大。建议使用一致且描述性的文字来定义选项。 * **规模选择**：0.8B 模型在速度与性能之间达到了最佳平衡；2B 模型虽在某些基准测试中得分略高，但在实际决策（如游戏）中表现得更为谨慎。 * **局限性**： * 仅支持英文和文本输入。 * 缺乏多步逻辑推理能力。 * Gemma 4 版本目前仍受限于 26 个选项的选择范围。
